title: I KNOW, MY SON, I KNOW

memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "But his father refused and said, 'I know, my son, I know. He too will become a people, and he too will become great. Nevertheless, his younger brother will be greater than he, and his descendants will become a group of nations.'" — Gen 48:19 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
"I know, my son, I know."

There is such gentleness in that repetition. Jacob is not annoyed at being corrected. He simply reassures his son: I understand what you are seeing, and I am doing this on purpose.

And then he blesses Manasseh anyway. "He too will become a people, and he too will become great." The one who received the lesser hand is not left with nothing. He gets a real, substantial blessing — just a different one.

That matters enormously. God's choosing does not mean rejection for everyone else. Manasseh became a full tribe with a full inheritance. He was not discarded because Ephraim received more.

We compare relentlessly. Someone else gets the greater gift, the wider opportunity, the more visible role, and we quietly conclude that we must have been passed over. But God is not running a competition where one person's blessing subtracts from yours.

Jesus made this point sharply in the parable of the vineyard workers, when those hired first grumbled at the generosity shown to others (Matt 20:15). God's generosity to another person is never a comment on His view of you.

I know, my son. He is doing it on purpose, and He has not forgotten you.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Where does comparison steal your gratitude?
2. Do you believe God has a real blessing for you, even if it is different?
3. Can you rejoice at someone else's greater gift?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, free me from measuring my life against someone else's. Thank You that Your generosity to others takes nothing from me. Help me receive what You have given with gratitude. Amen.
